newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds weaker on market fears over U.S. rates.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds weaker on market fears over U.S. rates.

text.p: Irish bonds were weaker in late trading on Thursday after fluctuating throughout the day in reaction to the release of key U.S inflation data, dealers said.
"We've seen fairly constant two-way trade today, largely switching up and down the curve," a dealer said.
"Irish bonds came off in response to the U.S. CPI figures, and then firmed on the more market-friendly Philly Fed survey and industrial production figures later on," he said.
The U.S. CPI data had raised expectations of a hike in U.S. rates at the next Federal Reserve meeting on May 20, dealers said.
Core inflation, or consumer prices ex food and energy, rose 0.3 percent against a 0.2 percent consensus forecast.

Trade in Irish bonds had been further complicated by the announcement early on Thursday by Ireland's National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) that it will auction 100 million punts of the 8.25 percent bond due 2015 on May 20.
The market had expected the announcement of a short-end bond for auction, dealers said.

"We'd anticipated a short-end bond and so had been selling during the week," a dealer said. "This left people short on the five-year, which is now outperforming the long-end, as you might expect ahead of the supply next week."

By 1515 GMT, the Irish 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down five pence from Tuesday's close at 102.50 to yield 5.83 percent, while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was down 10 pence from the close at 109.90 to yield 6.54 percent.
Elsewhere, gilts were also hurt by UK April retail prices, which rose 0.6 percent against a 0.6 percent forecast and 0.3 percent previously.
On Thursday, the NTMA also announced a non-competitive auction confined to primary dealers of up to 20 million punts following the competitive auction on May 20.
